The Case for Stronger Public Modesty Standards

Public spaces are shared spaces, and the clothing we choose to wear in them is not merely a private matter—it is a social act with real consequences for the communities we inhabit. While personal expression deserves respect, the pendulum in recent decades has swung so far toward individual license that we have forgotten the legitimate interests communities hold in maintaining a baseline of decorum in public life. Expanding public indecency laws to enforce meaningful standards of modesty—including reasonable regulation of extremely revealing attire in general public spaces—would serve the common good in several important ways.

Public Spaces Are Not Private Living Rooms

The first principle is simple: what is acceptable on private property is not automatically acceptable in public. We already accept this intuitively. Full nudity is prohibited almost everywhere, not because the human body is shameful, but because shared public environments require shared standards. Streets, parks, government buildings, shopping districts, and public transit are environments where citizens of every age, background, religion, and sensibility must coexist. A civilized society calibrates public norms to respect this diversity rather than privileging the preferences of the least modest.

The claim that "if you don't like it, don't look" inverts the logic of public space. Pedestrians cannot avert their eyes from everything around them, nor should children have to. The burden of adjustment belongs, at least partly, to those entering shared spaces, not only to those already using them.

Protecting Children and Families

Parents consistently report difficulty shielding young children from hypersexualized imagery in advertising, media, and increasingly, in daily public life. When extremely revealing clothing becomes normalized on main streets and in family areas, parents lose the ability to decide when and how to introduce certain topics to their children. Stronger public standards restore that authority to families. A child walking to school or to the library should be able to do so in an environment calibrated for their developmental stage.

This is not about shame; it is about age-appropriate environments, the same principle that justifies film ratings, restrictions on alcohol advertising near schools, and zoning of adult businesses.

Dignity, Not Repression

Critics will charge that modesty laws reduce people—particularly women—to objects in need of covering. The opposite is true. Cultures and legal systems that maintain reasonable modesty norms communicate that persons are more than bodies on display, and that human worth is not measured by visual exposure. A public culture saturated with the expectation of bodily display places enormous pressure, especially on young women and girls, to participate in that display in order to be seen as confident or valuable. Clear public standards relieve that pressure by removing the constant competitive dynamic.

Modesty norms, properly framed, are egalitarian: they apply to all and treat every citizen as a full person entering civic life, not as a spectacle.

Context-Sensitive, Not Puritanical

A sensible framework would not be uniform or absolute. Swimsuits at beaches and pools are entirely appropriate to those contexts—that is precisely the point. What is at issue is context: beachwear at the grocery store, see-through garments in government buildings, or extremely revealing attire in family parks. Context-sensitive regulations—already the norm for dress codes in courts, schools, and many workplaces—could be extended modestly to general public standards. Nightlife districts, private clubs, and beaches could retain more permissive norms. The goal is calibration, not uniformity.

Social Cohesion and Civic Respect

Shared norms of dress signal mutual respect among citizens. Just as we expect a certain volume level in public, a baseline of sobriety, and courtesy in queues, we can reasonably expect attire that reflects awareness of others. Clothing is a form of communication, and communication directed at a captive audience of strangers should meet a minimum standard of civility. Countries and communities that maintain such expectations often report stronger senses of public cohesion and lower everyday friction between strangers.

The strongest objection is that such laws infringe on personal freedom. But freedom in a republic has always been bounded by the equal freedom of others. We do not consider noise ordinances, public intoxication laws, or rules against public urination to be tyrannical; they are ordinary adjustments of individual conduct to shared life. Reasonable dress standards in specifically defined public contexts belong in the same category. They restrict almost nothing—a person retains complete freedom of dress at home, at beaches, in nightlife venues, and at private events.

Conclusion

A society that cannot ask anything of its members in shared spaces is not a free society but an atomized one. Expanding public indecency standards to include thoughtful, context-sensitive regulation of extremely revealing attire in general public spaces would protect children, reduce social pressure on young people, affirm human dignity over display, and restore a sense of shared civic life. This is not a call for repression but for balance—a recognition that the public square belongs to everyone, and that its norms should reflect that shared ownership rather than the preferences of the most exhibitionist among us.

Modesty, rightly understood, is not the enemy of freedom. It is one of its quiet supports.

It is crucial to understand these laws within a framework of human rights and gender equality. The international consensus, as reflected in documents like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Beijing Platform for Action, views coercive modesty laws as:

  1. A Form of Gender Discrimination: These laws disproportionately target and restrict women's bodies, autonomy, and freedom of expression. They often place the burden of preventing male desire and violence on women, rather than on potential perpetrators.
  2. Violation of Bodily Autonomy and Freedom of Expression: They represent state control over personal choices regarding clothing, hairstyle, and movement, which are fundamental aspects of individual identity and self-expression.
  3. Instrument of Patriarchal Control: Critics argue these laws are less about "morality" and more about maintaining patriarchal power structures by controlling women's sexuality and public presence.

  6. Political Tool: Such laws are frequently used to marginalize minorities, suppress dissent, and rally political support by creating an "us vs. them" cultural narrative.

Conclusion

While the stated reasons for strict public indecency laws center on morality, tradition, and social order, the supposed benefits (like reduced harassment) are widely debunked by evidence and human rights analysis. The overwhelming critique from international law and gender studies is that these laws function primarily as tools of social control, particularly over women, violating fundamental rights to autonomy, expression, and equality under the guise of protecting society. The debate ultimately pits communal/religious norms against individual liberties and gender equality—a profound tension seen in many societies around the world.

Reclaiming Public Decorum: The Case for Expanding Public Modesty Standards

Introduction

In an era of accelerating cultural permissiveness, the boundaries of acceptable public presentation have eroded to a degree that would have been unthinkable mere decades ago. What was once confined to private spaces or designated venues—revealing clothing, provocative attire, and displays of near-nudity—has become commonplace in shopping centers, parks, restaurants, and streets where families gather. I. The Legal Precedent and Philosophical Foundation

The argument for expanded modesty standards does not emerge from a vacuum. It builds upon a well-established legal tradition in virtually every democratic society on earth. Every nation, state, and municipality already enforces some threshold of public decency. Complete public nudity is prohibited in nearly all jurisdictions. Indecent exposure statutes exist across the developed world. The question, therefore, is not whether the state has the authority to regulate public bodily presentation—that question has been answered affirmatively for centuries—but rather where the line should be drawn.

The philosophical foundation for public decency regulation rests on a principle that John Stuart Mill himself acknowledged even within his famous harm principle: that the public sphere is a shared commons, and behaviors that substantially affect the character of that commons are legitimate subjects of collective governance. Mill distinguished between conduct that affects only the individual and conduct that affects others, and he acknowledged that public acts fall into the latter category. When one enters the public square, one's presentation becomes, by definition, a public matter.

Furthermore, the legal concept of "community standards," upheld repeatedly by courts including the United States Supreme Court in cases like Miller v. California (1973), affirms that communities possess the right to define and enforce norms of decency. The argument that these standards should be frozen at their current permissive threshold—but should never have been allowed to erode from their previous position—is arbitrary. If community standards can shift in one direction, they can be deliberately recalibrated in the other, provided due democratic process is followed.

Constitutional scholars have long recognized that freedom of expression, even where it encompasses elements of personal presentation, is not absolute. Time, place, and manner restrictions are entirely consistent with First Amendment jurisprudence. Requiring appropriate coverage in public spaces shared by all citizens—including children, the elderly, and those with deeply held religious or cultural values—represents precisely the kind of reasonable regulation that democratic societies have always maintained the authority to impose.

II. Protecting Children and Vulnerable Populations

Perhaps the most compelling argument for stricter public modesty standards centers on the protection of children. The modern public environment has become saturated with sexualized imagery and presentation to a degree that developmental psychologists have increasingly flagged as concerning. The American Psychological Association's Task Force on the Sexualization of Girls published a landmark report documenting the extensive harms of premature exposure to sexualized content, including increased rates of anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and diminished cognitive performance.

Children do not choose to enter the public sphere—they are brought there by necessity. A child walking through a public park, a shopping district, or a beach boardwalk has no mechanism for filtering the visual environment. When adults present themselves in clothing that leaves little to the imagination—string bikinis far from the beach, clothing that exposes undergarments, tops that barely contain the body—children are involuntarily exposed to sexualized presentations that they are developmentally unprepared to process.

Critics will argue that the human body is natural and that children should not be taught shame. But this argument conflates two distinct issues. Teaching children healthy body awareness is entirely compatible with maintaining that the deliberate public display of sexualized presentation is inappropriate for shared spaces. Every society in human history has maintained some distinction between private and public bodily presentation, and this universal norm exists precisely because human beings—including and especially developing children—process exposed sexuality in psychologically significant ways.

Moreover, the expansion of revealing public attire creates pressure on adolescents, particularly young girls, to adopt similar standards of presentation. When hypersexualized clothing becomes normalized in public spaces, teenagers internalize the message that their value is connected to their willingness to display their bodies. Stricter public modesty standards would relieve this pressure, creating an environment where young people are not compelled to compete in an escalating race toward exposure.

III. Restoring the Shared Commons

The public sphere is not a private stage. It is a shared resource that belongs equally to all citizens—the provocative and the modest, the young and the old, the secular and the religious. The current permissive regime effectively prioritizes the expressive preferences of those who wish to dress revealingly over the comfort, values, and sensibilities of those who find such displays objectionable, distressing, or incompatible with their deeply held beliefs.

This represents a fundamental asymmetry. Under the current system, a person who wishes to dress modestly can do so, but they cannot avoid being confronted with others' revealing attire in shared spaces. Meanwhile, the person who dresses revealingly enjoys both the freedom to present themselves as they choose and the power to impose that presentation on everyone around them. Expanded modesty standards would restore balance, creating public spaces that are genuinely inclusive—welcoming to people of all cultural backgrounds, religious traditions, and personal values.

Many devout Muslims, Orthodox Jews, conservative Christians, and adherents of numerous other religious and cultural traditions experience genuine distress when confronted with highly revealing clothing in public spaces. For these citizens, the current permissive environment functions as a form of exclusion—a message that the public sphere does not accommodate their values or their comfort. This is the same principle that underlies dress codes in courtrooms, places of worship, formal events, and many workplaces. The expectation of appropriate attire is understood in these contexts not as oppression but as a mark of respect for the occasion and for others present. Expanding this principle to general public spaces merely extends a logic that is already widely accepted.

The liberalization of public dress standards has not occurred in a vacuum. It has developed in tandem with the broader commercialization and commodification of sexuality—a process driven not by authentic liberation but by market forces that profit from the sexualization of public life. The fashion industry, advertising sector, and entertainment complex have powerful financial incentives to push the boundaries of public exposure ever further, because sexualized presentation drives consumption.

Expanded public modesty standards would disrupt this commercial cycle, creating space for individuals—particularly women and girls—to develop self-presentation norms that are not dictated by industries profiting from their exposure.

Modesty legislation, far from oppressing women, could liberate them from the relentless expectation that their bodies must be publicly performed.

An important clarification is warranted: the argument for expanded modesty standards is not an argument for burqas, for the elimination of swimwear at beaches, or for a puritanical regime that denies the reality of the human form. Rather, it is an argument for context-appropriate standards that recognize the distinction between venues and occasions.

"This violates individual freedom." All law constrains individual freedom in the service of collective well-being. Speed limits constrain freedom of movement. The question is never whether freedom should be limited but where the limits should fall. The Case for Standards

Stricter public indecency laws are not about controlling individuals. They are about honoring a social contract. When you step into a public space—a space shared by families, by children, by the elderly, by people of faith, by people of every background—you enter into an unspoken agreement: I will conduct myself with respect for those around me.

Public decency laws are the guardrails of that agreement.

Consider what we already accept without controversy: we regulate noise in residential neighborhoods. We enforce building codes. We maintain health standards in restaurants. We do these things not because we are tyrants, but because shared spaces require shared responsibility.

Why, then, should we abandon standards when it comes to personal conduct and presentation in those very same spaces?

Modesty Is Not Weakness

Somewhere along the way, our culture began to confuse modesty with repression and exhibitionism with liberation. Let me say clearly: modesty is a virtue, not a limitation.

Modesty reflects self-respect. It reflects an awareness that we exist in relation to others. It reflects the understanding that not every private expression belongs in the public square.

The great moral traditions that built our communities—traditions spanning faiths and philosophies—have consistently valued temperance, restraint, and dignity in public life. These are not antiquated relics. They are the foundations upon which trust between neighbors is built.

When we allow public spaces to become stages for increasingly provocative and indecent behavior, we do not expand freedom—we erode the freedom of families to move through their own communities without being subjected to content they did not choose and cannot avoid.

A person of faith should not be made to feel like a stranger in their own country for holding standards that were mainstream within living memory.

The Erosion Is Real

Let us be honest about what has happened. Standards have not simply evolved—they have collapsed.

What was considered indecent on public airwaves twenty years ago is now considered tame. What would have drawn concern in a public space a generation ago now draws nothing more than a shrug. And each time the line moves, we are told: this is progress.

But progress toward what?

Has the coarsening of public life made our communities stronger? Has the abandonment of modesty norms made our young people more confident, more secure, more respectful of themselves and others?

The evidence says otherwise. We see rising anxiety among young people. We see the erosion of respect in public discourse. We see communities fragmenting because the common ground—the shared sense of this is how we conduct ourselves together—has been stripped away.

A society that cannot define the boundaries of acceptable public conduct is a society that has lost confidence in its own values.

What We Propose

Let me be specific about what stronger public indecency laws would mean—and what they would not mean.

They would mean:

  • Clear, enforceable standards for conduct and attire in public spaces, particularly those frequented by families and children
  • Meaningful consequences for lewd or deliberately provocative behavior in parks, streets, public events, and government spaces
  • Empowering local communities to establish standards that reflect their values through democratic processes
  • Strengthened protections for children from exposure to adult content in public settings
  • Supporting law enforcement with clear guidelines to address indecent conduct consistently and fairly

They would NOT mean:

  • Government agents policing fashion choices in private establishments
  • Theocratic mandates imposed without democratic consent
  • Targeting any specific group, culture, or identity
  • Eliminating artistic expression or legitimate free discourse

Now, I know the objections. I've heard them all.

With respect—that is exactly what law does. Every law reflects a moral judgment. Laws against theft reflect the moral judgment that property should be respected. Laws against assault reflect the moral judgment that bodily autonomy matters. Public decency laws reflect the moral judgment that shared spaces deserve a baseline of respect.

"This is a slippery slope toward authoritarianism."

No. A slippery slope runs in both directions. The complete absence of public standards leads to a different kind of tyranny—one where the most brazen behavior dominates and the majority who desire order and decency are silenced by the accusation that they are intolerant for expecting any standards at all.

"Times change."

"Who decides what's decent?"

We do. Together. Through the democratic process. Through elected representatives accountable to their communities. That is how self-governing people have always set standards—not by surrendering the question entirely and pretending that no standards are needed.

These are not burdens. They are gifts.

And defending them in the public square—through reasonable, democratically enacted laws—is not oppression. It is stewardship.

We stand at a crossroads, and the choice is straightforward:

We can continue down a path where every standard is questioned, every norm is deconstructed, and every call for decency is dismissed as backward—until we wake up in communities where nothing is sacred, nothing is shared, and nothing holds us together.

Stricter public indecency laws are not the entirety of what we need. Cultural renewal begins in homes, in houses of worship, in schools, and in the daily choices of individuals who refuse to surrender their principles to the pressure of a permissive age.

But law matters. Law sets expectations. Law draws lines. Law tells a society: this is who we are, and this is what we will not accept.

Let them know that the silent majority that believes in decency, in modesty, in the conservative values that built these communities is silent no more.

We are not asking for anything radical. We are asking for something ancient, proven, and profoundly necessary.

We are asking for decency.

We are asking for standards.

We are asking for the courage to defend them.

Thank you, and God bless our communities, our families, and the values that hold them together.
